*Early Life and Captivity*
Raymond III was born around 1140. He was the son of Raymond II of Tripoli and Hodierna of Jerusalem. His father was assassinated in 1152. Raymond then became Count of Tripoli as a child. His mother Hodierna likely helped govern the county during his minority. In 1160 Nur ad-Din Zengi captured Raymond. He spent about thirteen years in captivity in Aleppo. He was released in 1173. His long imprisonment shaped his cautious diplomacy. He learned to value truces and negotiation with Muslim powers.

*Marriage and Galilee*
After his release Raymond married Eschiva of Bures in 1174. Eschiva was the Princess of Galilee and Lady of Tiberias. Through this marriage Raymond became Prince of Galilee and Lord of Tiberias. These titles gave him great influence in the Kingdom of Jerusalem. He also became a leading member of the High Court. The High Court was the kingdom's chief feudal council. Raymond used his position to defend baronial rights against royal favorites.

*Regent of Jerusalem*
King Amalric died in 1174. His son Baldwin IV was a child and a leper. Raymond became regent for Baldwin IV. He served from 1174 to 1177. He tried to secure the kingdom's borders and manage its factions. Later Baldwin IV married Sibylla to Guy of Lusignan. Guy became a rival to Raymond. In 1183 Baldwin IV made Guy regent. Then Baldwin IV removed Guy. Baldwin IV crowned his nephew Baldwin V as co-king. When Baldwin IV died in 1185 Raymond became regent for Baldwin V. Baldwin V died in 1186. Raymond opposed the coronation of Sibylla and Guy. He withdrew to Tiberias. He and other nobles challenged the new royal couple.

*Later Years and Death*
Raymond made a controversial truce with Saladin. In 1187 Saladin invaded the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Raymond advised King Guy not to march to relieve Tiberias. Guy ignored this advice. The crusader army met Saladin at the Battle of Hattin. Raymond commanded part of the army. He and Balian of Ibelin broke through Saladin's lines. They escaped. Raymond died later in 1187. He died in Tripoli. He had no legitimate children. His county passed to Raymond IV. Raymond III left a mixed legacy. Some saw him as a skilled survivor. Others saw him as a self-interested lord. His career showed the deep divisions of the Crusader states before Hattin.

Hark! Good traveler I have wrought for thee a scroll of Nippon. Let these days unfold like petals in a bard's tale.

First Day: Tokyo  
Arrive at Haneda or Narita. Take the train unto the city. Walk Shinjuku's lantern-lit lanes. Eat a bowl of ramen. Rest thy weary bones.

Second Day: Tokyo  
At dawn seek Tsukiji Outer Market. Then visit Senso-ji in Asakusa. Wander Ueno Park. In evening go to Shibuya Crossing. Behold the neon tide.

Third Day: Tokyo to Hakone  
Ride a train to Hakone. Sail Lake Ashi. See Mount Fuji if fortune smiles. Soak in an onsen. Return to Tokyo or stay.

Fourth Day: Tokyo to Kyoto  
Board the shinkansen. Watch the land fly. Arrive in Kyoto. Stroll Gion. Seek geisha shadows. Sleep in a ryokan.

Fifth Day: Kyoto  
Visit Fushimi Inari at dawn. Climb the torii gates. Then see Kinkaku-ji. Wander Arashiyama. Cross the bamboo grove. Dine on tofu and sake.

Sixth Day: Nara  
Take a train to Nara. Feed the bowing deer. See Todai-ji's great Buddha. Return to Kyoto. Rest.

Seventh Day: Kyoto to Osaka  
Travel to Osaka. See Osaka Castle. Eat takoyaki. Wander Dotonbori. Laugh at the blazing signs.

Journey to Kanazawa. See Kenroku-en. Walk the samurai district. Taste gold leaf ice cream. Sleep.

Tenth Day: Kanazawa to Tokyo  
Return to Tokyo by train. Buy strange sweets. See a kabuki play if thou canst. Raise a final cup. Then homeward bound.

resps:
# The Surprising Benefits of Sleeping in a Hammock

When most people picture a hammock, they imagine a lazy summer afternoon: a cold drink, a good book, and maybe a short nap. But hammocks are more than a relaxing accessory. For campers, backpackers, and even everyday sleepers, sleeping overnight in a hammock can offer a surprising range of benefits, from deep relaxation to better back support. If you’ve never considered trading your mattress for a suspended bed, here’s why it might be worth trying.

## 1. Pressure relief and spinal support

A well-hung hammock cradles the body and distributes weight evenly, reducing pressure on the shoulders, hips, and heels. Unlike a firm mattress that can create concentrated pressure points, a hammock conforms to your shape. When you lie diagonally—at a slight angle rather than curled up like a banana—you can lie relatively flat, allowing your spine to rest in a more natural alignment. Many people with mild back pain report feeling better after sleeping in a hammock, though anyone with serious back issues should consult a doctor first.

## 2. Gentle rocking promotes deeper sleep

The gentle sway of a hammock is soothing. That motion can help activate the parasympathetic nervous system, shifting your body out of fight-or-flight mode and into rest-and-digest mode. It’s similar to the way a rocking cradle helps babies fall asleep. For adults, that rhythmic movement can mean falling asleep faster, waking less often, and enjoying a more restorative night.

## 3. Cooler, better-ventilated sleep

Because a hammock lifts you off the ground, air circulates underneath you. On warm nights, that airflow can keep you cooler than a tent floor or mattress, which tends to trap heat. In colder weather, you can add an underquilt or pad for insulation. This versatility makes hammocks comfortable across a wide range of temperatures—especially for camping.

## 4. Lightweight, portable, and campsite-friendly

For campers and backpackers, hammocks are a game-changer. They’re lightweight, pack small, and don’t require a flat, rock-free patch of ground. As long as you have two sturdy trees or posts, you have a bed. That means you can camp in places where tents won’t work, reduce your impact on delicate ground, and set up or pack away in minutes.

## 5. A closer connection to nature

Sleeping in a hammock outdoors can deepen your connection to the natural world. You may hear owls, feel a breeze, and wake with the sunrise. That exposure to natural light and fresh air can help regulate your circadian rhythm and improve mood. Even indoors, a hammock creates a cozy, screen-free spot to unwind, read, or meditate.

## 6. Space-saving and versatile

Hammocks take up very little room. In a small apartment, they can replace a bulky guest bed or sofa. Outdoors, they turn any pair of trees into a relaxing retreat. You can use them for camping, travel, backyard naps, or simply as a unique place to relax after work.

## A few tips for better hammock sleep

To get the most out of hammock sleeping, hang it with a gentle sag—about a 30-degree angle—and lie diagonally. Use a bug net, an underquilt in cold weather, and check that your supports are strong and safe. Practice at home before committing to a full night outdoors.

## Final thoughts

Sleeping in a hammock isn’t for everyone, and it takes some adjustment. But for many people, it offers pressure relief, deep relaxation, cooler sleep, and a sense of adventure. Whether you’re thru-hiking a trail or just looking for a better afternoon nap, a hammock might be the most comfortable bed you’ve never tried.

Ethan woke to the same ceiling he’d seen for thirty-four years, but the morning light had a thin, pixelated edge. When he reached for his glasses, a translucent inventory panel blinked at the corner of his vision, listing “Glasses (Common)” and “Left Sock (Missing).” He sat up slowly, and the room around him hummed with invisible machinery; the wall clock ticked backward for one second, then corrected itself. Outside his window, birds repeated the same three-note loop, and a neighbor froze mid-wave when Ethan looked directly at her, as if waiting for him to move away from the camera.

***

By noon he had tested the rules: he couldn’t open doors without pressing his palm to them until a blue progress bar filled, and every time he lied, a red “-5 Trust” floated above the other person’s head. He tried to scream, but only preset dialogue options appeared on his tongue. Then, in the bathroom mirror, he saw not his own tired face but a character model with a name tag reading “PLAYER_1,” and beneath it, a tiny line of text: “Press any key to continue.” Ethan laughed until it hurt, or until the laugh animation ended, and he understood that the only way out was to stop being the one holding the controller.

resps:
the social network (2010) is not really a movie about how facebook was founded. it is a movie about what founding something does to the people who found it. david fincher directs a screenplay by aaron sorkin, and the film turns a story of servers, code, and lawsuits into a shakespearean tragedy for the internet age. it is cold, fast, funny, cruel, and unexpectedly moving. it also remains one of the best films of the 21st century about ambition, class, friendship, and the loneliness that can come from connecting everyone.

the plot is framed by two depositions. in one, mark zuckerberg is being sued by eduardo saverin, his former best friend and facebook's first chief financial officer. in the other, he is being sued by the winklevoss twins and divya narendra, who claim he stole their idea for a harvard social network. between these legal scenes, the film flashes back to 2003, when mark is a sophomore at harvard. after his girlfriend erica albright breaks up with him, he goes back to his dorm, drinks, and writes a cruel blog post about her. he then creates facemash, a site that lets users compare and rate female students. the site crashes harvard's servers, but it also gets attention. the winklevoss twins, wealthy rowers and identical twins, recruit mark to help build harvard connection, a dating site for harvard students. mark stalls them and instead builds thefacebook with money from eduardo. when sean parker, the founder of napster, enters the story, the company shifts to palo alto, eduardo gets diluted, and the friendships that made the site possible begin to collapse.

what makes the film so strong is that it refuses easy villains. mark is not a monster in a cape. he is a brilliant, insecure, socially awkward young man who wants to be seen and respected. his cruelty is not separate from his genius; it is part of the same hunger. eduardo is not a saint either. he is proud, conventional, and sometimes blind to how the world is changing. sean parker is charismatic and dangerous, a prophet of a new economy who also represents its worst excesses. the film understands that everyone in this story is trying to prove something. mark wants to prove he is not a nobody. eduardo wants to prove he belongs. the twins want to prove they were wronged. sean wants to prove he can still matter. and the lawyers just want to close the case.

sorkin's screenplay is famous for its speed and wit, and it deserves the praise. the dialogue overlaps, snaps, and cuts. characters insult each other with the precision of fencing masters. but the script is not just clever. it is structured like a tragedy. the opening breakup scene tells you everything. mark cannot stop talking, cannot stop analyzing, cannot stop trying to win an argument that is not a debate. erica tells him that he will go through life thinking girls do not like him because he is a nerd, but really it will be because he is an asshole. that line hangs over the entire film. mark spends the rest of the movie proving her right while also proving that he is not simply a jerk. he is a person who has built a machine for avoiding the intimacy he cannot handle.

fincher's direction is perfect for this material. he shoots the film in cool, muted colors. harvard feels old, exclusive, and slightly hostile. palo alto feels sunny but empty. the deposition rooms are sterile and gray. the camera moves with precision, and the editing by kirk baxter is astonishing. the film cuts between past and present, between parties and lawsuits, between creation and consequence. the result is a kind of rhythmic anxiety. even when characters are just sitting and talking, the film feels like a thriller. trent reznor and atticus ross provide a score that is not traditional. it is ambient, electronic, pulsing, and unsettling. it sounds like the hum of a server farm and the static of a lonely mind.

the performances are uniformly excellent. jesse eisenberg's mark is a career-defining turn. he speaks quickly, blinks rarely, and holds his face in a mask of superiority that barely hides his hurt. he makes mark watchable without making him likable. andrew garfield's eduardo is the emotional center of the film. he is warm, loyal, and increasingly desperate. his betrayal feels genuinely painful because garfield lets you see the friendship before it rots. justin timberlake's sean parker is a live wire. he is seductive, manic, and full of bad ideas delivered with perfect confidence. armie hammer plays both cameron and tyler winklevoss, and he gives each twin a distinct energy. rooney mara's erica is only in a few scenes, but she is unforgettable. rashida jones as marilyn delpy, one of mark's lawyers, gets the film's most devastating line, and she delivers it with quiet weariness.

the film is not a documentary. it takes liberties with the facts. the real mark zuckerberg has disputed many details. the real eduardo saverin has his own version. the winklevoss twins have their own version. sorkin and fincher compress events, invent conversations, and sharpen motivations for dramatic effect. this bothers some viewers, and it is fair to note. but the film is not pretending to be a court transcript. it is after emotional truth. it wants to capture the feeling of a certain moment in tech history: the moment when a website built in a dorm room became a global empire, and the people who built it discovered that friendship, loyalty, and ownership are not the same thing.

the social network also has a complicated legacy. it won three academy awards, for best adapted screenplay, best original score, and best film editing. it was nominated for best picture, best director, and best actor. it did not win best picture, which remains one of the more debated oscars of the 2010s. it made a generation of viewers care about depositions, cap tables, and term sheets. it also helped define a new genre of tech cinema, though few later films matched its icy precision. some critics argue that the women in the film are underdeveloped, and that is a valid criticism. erica and marilyn are sharp, but they exist mostly to illuminate mark. others argue that the film ends too early. it stops before facebook's darkest chapters: privacy scandals, misinformation, election interference, and the broader question of what happens when a social network becomes social infrastructure. but that is also the point. the film is about the creation myth, not the aftermath. it asks how the thing was made, and what it cost the people who made it.

the final scene is one of the loneliest in modern cinema. mark sits alone in a conference room, after the depositions, and sends a friend request to erica. then he refreshes the page. he waits. the screen glows. the score hums. he is the most connected man in the world, and he is completely alone. it is a perfect ending because it does not offer redemption or punishment. it just shows the shape of his life. he built a machine for connection, and he cannot connect. he won the argument, and he lost the thing he actually wanted.

the social network is not a perfect film. it is too neat in places, too cruel in others, and too willing to sacrifice fact for drama. but as a piece of storytelling, it is extraordinary. it is a movie about a website, but it is also about class, envy, betrayal, and the American dream in its digital form. it is about how the desire to be included can turn into the desire to control inclusion. it is about how smart people can be stupid about love. and it is about how the things we build to escape loneliness can become the walls that keep us alone. if you want a factual account, read the books and the lawsuits. if you want a great film about ambition, friendship, and the price of being right, watch this. it remains essential, unsettling, and endlessly quotable.

fincher's direction is perfect for this material. he shoots the film in cool, muted colors. harvard feels old, exclusive, and slightly hostile. palo alto feels sunny but empty. the deposition rooms are sterile and gray. the camera moves with precision, and the editing by kirk baxter is astonishing. the film cuts between past and present, between parties and lawsuits, between creation and consequence. the result is a kind of rhythmic anxiety. even when characters are just sitting and talking, the film feels like a thriller. trent reznor and atticus ross provide a score that is not traditional. it is ambient, electronic, pulsing, and unsettling. it sounds like the hum of a server farm and the static of a lonely mind.

the performances are uniformly excellent. jesse eisenberg's mark is a career-defining turn. he speaks quickly, blinks rarely, and holds his face in a mask of superiority that barely hides his hurt. he makes mark watchable without making him likable. andrew garfield's eduardo is the emotional center of the film. he is warm, loyal, and increasingly desperate. his betrayal feels genuinely painful because garfield lets you see the friendship before it rots. justin timberlake's sean parker is a live wire. he is seductive, manic, and full of bad ideas delivered with perfect confidence. armie hammer plays both cameron and tyler winklevoss, and he gives each twin a distinct energy. rooney mara's erica is only in a few scenes, but she is unforgettable. rashida jones as marilyn delpy, one of mark's lawyers, gets the film's most devastating line, and she delivers it with quiet weariness.

the film is not a documentary. it takes liberties with the facts. the real mark zuckerberg has disputed many details. the real eduardo saverin has his own version. the winklevoss twins have their own version. sorkin and fincher compress events, invent conversations, and sharpen motivations for dramatic effect. this bothers some viewers, and it is fair to note. but the film is not pretending to be a court transcript. it is after emotional truth. it wants to capture the feeling of a certain moment in tech history: the moment when a website built in a dorm room became a global empire, and the people who built it discovered that friendship, loyalty, and ownership are not the same thing.

the social network also has a complicated legacy. it won three academy awards, for best adapted screenplay, best original score, and best film editing. it was nominated for best picture, best director, and best actor. it did not win best picture, which remains one of the more debated oscars of the 2010s. it made a generation of viewers care about depositions, cap tables, and term sheets. it also helped define a new genre of tech cinema, though few later films matched its icy precision. some critics argue that the women in the film are underdeveloped, and that is a valid criticism. erica and marilyn are sharp, but they exist mostly to illuminate mark. others argue that the film ends too early. it stops before facebook's darkest chapters: privacy scandals, misinformation, election interference, and the broader question of what happens when a social network becomes social infrastructure. but that is also the point. the film is about the creation myth, not the aftermath. it asks how the thing was made, and what it cost the people who made it.

the final scene is one of the loneliest in modern cinema. mark sits alone in a conference room, after the depositions, and sends a friend request to erica. then he refreshes the page. he waits. the screen glows. the score hums. he is the most connected man in the world, and he is completely alone. it is a perfect ending because it does not offer redemption or punishment. it just shows the shape of his life. he built a machine for connection, and he cannot connect. he won the argument, and he lost the thing he actually wanted.

the social network is not a perfect film. it is too neat in places, too cruel in others, and too willing to sacrifice fact for drama. but as a piece of storytelling, it is extraordinary. it is a movie about a website, but it is also about class, envy, betrayal, and the American dream in its digital form. it is about how the desire to be included can turn into the desire to control inclusion. it is about how smart people can be stupid about love. and it is about how the things we build to escape loneliness can become the walls that keep us alone. if you want a factual account, read the books and the lawsuits. if you want a great film about ambition, friendship, and the price of being right, watch this. it remains essential, unsettling, and endlessly quotable.

**Japan, Day by Day**

I landed in Tokyo with a suitcase, a rail pass, and no real plan. That turned out to be the best way to travel.

Tokyo was neon and quiet corners. I ate ramen at a tiny counter in Shinjuku, wandered through Senso-ji at dawn, and got happily lost in Shibuya Crossing. Every convenience store became a treasure hunt: onigiri, matcha KitKats, and egg sandwiches I still think about.

Then the shinkansen carried me to Kyoto. Old wooden temples, bamboo groves, and streets that smelled like incense. I rented a bike and pedaled past rivers and shrines, stopping for matcha ice cream whenever I needed a break. In Nara, deer bowed for crackers. In Osaka, I ate takoyaki that burned my mouth and didn’t care.

The quietest moment came in Hakone. I soaked in an onsen while Mount Fuji hid behind clouds, then appeared for ten perfect minutes. No photo could capture it.

What surprised me most wasn’t the technology or the cherry blossoms. It was the kindness. A stranger walked me to the right train. A shop owner drew a map on a napkin. A conductor bowed as the train left.

Japan isn’t just a place you visit. It’s a place that rearranges something inside you. I came home with a heavier suitcase, a lighter heart, and a list of reasons to return.

If you’re thinking of going: go. Get the rail pass. Learn “arigatou.” Say yes to the strange little alley. You won’t regret it.

<<Why Cows Become Food and Worms Become Contamination>>
Response 1: Culture and categorization shape disgust. Many people are taught that cows are livestock and beef is a normal, safe food, while worms are pests, parasites, or signs of rot and filth. Its early rulers, especially Taizong and Xuanzong, expanded the empire, but expansion often meant war. Tang armies fought a series of campaigns against the Eastern Turks, Western Turks, Goguryeo, and Tibetan powers; each war strained resources, yet victories could bring peace. After Li Yuan founded the dynasty, the Tang consolidated power through civil war and then imposed a durable internal peace. Taizong’s reign, called Zhenguan, is idealized as a time of good government and relative peace. The Tang code and exam system helped maintain peace among elites and provinces. Along the Silk Road, commerce flourished because a degree of peace allowed merchants, monks, and envoys to travel. Wu Zetian’s rise brought political intrigue and some war, but also administrative continuity and periods of peace. Under Xuanzong’s Kaiyuan era, China reached a cultural peak and a long peace, though frontier war continued intermittently. The An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) shattered that peace; it was a devastating civil war that weakened the dynasty. After the rebellion, Tang rulers struggled to restore peace, while regional warlords and border conflicts meant recurring war. The later Tang saw Huang Chao’s rebellion, another destructive war, and the final collapse in 907 ended the dynasty’s peace. Even so, Tang influence in law, poetry, religion, and trade lasted far beyond its fall, shaping East Asia in times of both war and peace.

resps:
"At the end of the nineteenth century, the state that many contemporaries still called the Austrian Empire was in fact the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy created by the 1867 Compromise. For Croats and Serbs, therefore, attitudes toward Austria were never simple. They were shaped by where a person lived, by religion, class, and political party, and by whether Vienna or Budapest was the immediate authority. The Croatian and Serbian nations were not unified political bodies: Croats lived in Croatia-Slavonia under the Hungarian crown, in Austrian-ruled Dalmatia and Istria, in the Military Frontier until its abolition in 1881, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina under Austro-Hungarian occupation after 1878. Serbs lived in independent Serbia, in Vojvodina under Hungary, in Croatia-Slavonia, in Dalmatia, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their sentiments toward the Habsburg/Austrian state thus ranged from loyalism and pragmatic acceptance to autonomy demands, federalist hopes, and outright anti-Habsburg nationalism.

For many Croats, the central political grievance was not Vienna alone but the dualist system that subordinated Croatia-Slavonia to Budapest. The Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868, known as the Nagodba, granted Croatia limited autonomy in internal affairs but left the Ban, the chief executive, appointed by the king on the recommendation of the Hungarian government. Hungarian was imposed in railways, administration, and some schools; Magyarization pressures grew, especially under Ban Khuen-Héderváry after 1883. Consequently, many Croatian nationalists looked to Vienna as a potential counterweight to Hungarian domination. This was the old logic of Austro-Slavism: the Habsburg dynasty might be persuaded to reorganize the monarchy into a federal or trialist state in which Croatia would have an equal South Slav unit. Bishop Josip Juraj Strossmayer and the National Party represented a moderate, liberal, and culturally Yugoslav-oriented current that could cooperate with the dynasty while opposing Hungarian centralism. Catholic clergy and conservative nobles often felt a dynastic loyalty to the emperor-king as a Catholic sovereign and a guarantor of order. Peasants, too, could be loyal to the person of the emperor while resenting taxes, military conscription, and arrogant local officials.

Yet Croatian sentiment was also strongly anti-Habsburg in important currents. The Party of Rights, inspired by Ante Starčević, denied the legitimacy of the dualist arrangement and emphasized Croatian state right. It regarded the Habsburgs as foreign rulers who had failed to protect Croatian interests and dreamed of an independent Croatia or, at least, a reorganised monarchy based on trialism. By the 1890s, Josip Frank's Pure Party of Rights had become more pragmatic and pro-Habsburg in the hope that Vienna would support a Croatian entity against Budapest, but this did not mean affection for Austrian centralism. In Dalmatia, Croatian nationalists under Austrian rule demanded unification with Croatia-Slavonia and complained of German and Italian dominance in local administration and education. At the same time, many Dalmatian Croats valued Austrian rule as a shield against Italian irredentism and were slower to embrace radical anti-Habsburg politics. The 1895 visit of Emperor Franz Joseph to Zagreb and the student burning of the Hungarian flag showed how quickly dynastic ceremonial could turn into nationalist protest against Hungarian rule.

Serbian attitudes were similarly layered but tended to be more sharply anti-Austrian, especially in Bosnia and in the independent Serbian state. Within the Habsburg Monarchy, Serbs possessed important collective privileges, particularly Orthodox Church autonomy and a strong confessional identity. In Vojvodina, however, the 1867 Compromise and later administrative reforms eroded Serbian political autonomy and exposed Serbs to Magyarization. The Serbian National Party demanded territorial and cultural autonomy, and Serbian intelligentsia, clergy, and merchants often looked to the emperor as a protector against Hungarian pressure. In Croatia-Slavonia, Serbs sometimes cooperated with Croatian opposition parties against Budapest, but they also feared Croatian assimilation and insisted on their own national identity. The Ban's divide-and-rule policies could temporarily favour Serbs as a counterweight to Croats, which deepened mutual suspicions. In Dalmatia, Serbs and Croats sometimes cooperated in a broader South Slav cultural politics, but Serbs retained a distinct Orthodox and Serbian national consciousness.

In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Austro-Hungarian occupation of 1878 was widely seen by Serbs as an act of foreign conquest. Serb peasants, Orthodox clergy, and merchants resented the new administration, taxes, conscription, and agrarian arrangements that often favoured Muslim landlords and Catholic officials. The 1878 uprising and the Herzegovina revolt of 1882 demonstrated that resistance. Austrian governor Benjamin Kállay tried to cultivate a Bosnian nation that would be loyal to the monarchy and would divide Serbs from Croats, but Serbian national activists increasingly saw Austria-Hungary as the main obstacle to union with Serbia. For them, Bosnia was Serbian land, and Habsburg rule was a temporary occupation to be ended. This anti-Austrian sentiment was reinforced by the network of Serbian schools, newspapers, and cultural societies that kept national consciousness alive.

In the Kingdom of Serbia, attitudes toward Austria were contradictory. The Obrenović dynasty, especially Prince Milan, signed a secret convention with Austria in 1881 and oriented Serbian foreign policy toward Vienna. Austria supported Serbia's territorial expansion to the south in 1878 and restrained it in the Serbo-Bulgarian War of 1885. For the court and some conservative politicians, Austria was a necessary great-power patron. But this Austrophile policy was unpopular among nationalists, radicals, and Russophiles. The Radical Party of Nikola Pašić looked to Russia and opposed Austrian economic and political domination. The older ideology of Nacertanije envisaged Serbia as a Piedmont that would liberate and unite all Serbs, including those in Bosnia, Herzegovina, Old Serbia, and Macedonia. Since Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia and blocked Serbian access to the Adriatic, it appeared as the chief enemy of that project. By the late 1890s and around 1900, anti-Austrian feeling in Serbian public life was rising, even though the government still tried to balance between Vienna and St Petersburg.

Religion and great-power orientation sharpened the contrast. Catholic Croats often saw the Habsburg dynasty as a historic Catholic power and a defence against Orthodox Russia and Magyar liberalism. Orthodox Serbs more often saw Russia as their protector and Austria as a Catholic and centralising empire. Yet neither nation was monolithic. Croats produced loyalist autonomists, Austro-Slav federalists, trialists, Party of Rights nationalists, and early Yugoslavists. Serbs produced Habsburg loyalists, Serbian autonomists in Vojvodina, Bosnian resistance activists, and independent Serbian nationalists. What united the more advanced nationalist circles was a rejection of dualist centralism and a demand for national self-determination. What divided them was whether the Habsburg Monarchy could be reformed into a federal or trialist state or whether it had to be dismantled.

By the end of the nineteenth century, therefore, sentiments toward the Austrian Empire and the wider Habsburg Monarchy were ambivalent and changing. Among Croats, resentment of Budapest often made Vienna look like a possible ally, but disappointment with dualism and Magyarization fed anti-Habsburg nationalism. Among Serbs, loyalty to the emperor in Habsburg lands coexisted with a powerful anti-Austrian current centred on Bosnia and the independent Serbian state. The period also saw the beginnings of Croatian-Serbian cooperation, which would become more visible in the Rijeka and Zadar resolutions of 1905. Still, mutual suspicions, competing national programmes, and the divide-and-rule policies of both Budapest and Vienna prevented a single South Slav response. The overall trend was away from passive dynastic loyalty and toward modern mass nationalism, in which the Habsburg Monarchy was increasingly seen either as an obsolete prison of peoples or as a framework that must be radically federalised if it were to survive."

resps:
"**From ARPANET to TikTok: How the Internet Changed Everything (Including Your Life)**

Hey, teens! Imagine waking up tomorrow with no Wi-Fi. No group chats. No TikTok. No YouTube, no Minecraft servers, no Google. You would probably feel like you lost a superpower. But the internet was not always in your pocket. It started as a small experiment and grew into the thing that shapes your day, your identity, and your future.

**The internet’s origin story**

In 1969, a U.S. government project called ARPANET connected four computers. The first message was supposed to be LOGIN. Instead, the system crashed after just two letters: LO. So the first internet message was basically 'LO' — like 'lol' without the rest. Not exactly viral, but it was a start.

In the 1970s, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn created TCP/IP, a set of rules that let different networks talk to each other. In 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP. Many people call that the internet’s birthday. The 1980s brought DNS, which made addresses easier to remember, and NSFNET, which connected universities and expanded access.

Then in 1991, Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN. He made the first website and gave us browsers, links, and HTML. By the mid-1990s, dial-up internet, AOL, chat rooms, and the dot-com boom arrived. It was slow, noisy, and magical.

**From desktops to your pocket**

The 2000s exploded. Broadband, Wi-Fi, Google, Wikipedia, MySpace, Facebook, and YouTube changed how we shared life. In 2007, the iPhone put the internet in our pockets. Communication: You can talk to anyone, anywhere, instantly. Group chats, DMs, and video calls keep friendships alive. But FOMO, cyberbullying, and constant pressure are real too.

Entertainment: Streaming, gaming, and memes are huge. Creators can become stars from their bedroom. But algorithms can keep you scrolling longer than you planned.

Identity and community: You can find people who get you. LGBTQ+ teens, fandoms, and niche hobby groups have safe spaces online. But echo chambers can make the world feel more divided.

Activism: You can organize, raise awareness, and start movements. But slacktivism and fake news can weaken real change.

Mental health: The internet can comfort and connect you. It can also make you compare yourself to filtered lives, lose sleep, and feel addicted.

Privacy: Your data is valuable. Companies track you, and anything you post can live forever. Sexting, nudes, and old posts can come back later.

Access: Not everyone has fast internet or a good device. The digital divide is real, and it affects school, jobs, and opportunity.

Think before you post. Screenshots live forever.

Check sources. If it sounds wild, verify it.

Protect your privacy. Strong passwords, two-factor authentication, and no sharing your address.

Balance screen time. Sleep, hobbies, and offline friends matter.

Be kind. Behind every username is a real person.

Use the internet for good. Learn a skill, build a portfolio, start a cause, or create something original.

The internet is not good or bad by itself. It is a tool. You are the first generation that grew up fully online, which means you have more power than you think. resps:
# The Eucalyptus Singing

Out of the dry and sun-scorched earth,
where the red dust dreams of rain,
they rise—the eucalypts—
like pillars of a green cathedral,
their bark peeling in long ribbons,
pale as moonlight, warm as amber,
leaving behind a skin of shadow
that curls at the foot of the trunk.

Their leaves hang down like slender blades,
silver-green, sickle-shaped,
turning always their edges to the sun,
so the light slips through them
in coins and whispers,
and the whole tree shimmers
as if it were a cloud
that learned to stand.

In the early morning, the scent arrives first:
a cool, sharp breath of menthol and honey,
eucalyptus and rain-washed wind,
a fragrance that opens the lungs
and clears the mind,
as if the tree were a medicine chest
rooted in the ground.

The koalas know its branches,
climbing slowly through the fragrant maze,
sleeping in forks of ancient limbs,
while honeyeaters stitch the air
with bright thread,
and parrots scatter like emeralds
through the crown.

But the eucalyptus is more than a picture.
It is a worker with a hundred hands.
Its timber is tough, durable, true—
fence posts, railway sleepers, decks, and floors,
boats that cut through salt and foam,
furniture that holds the warmth of home.

Its pulp becomes paper:
the page of a poem,
the map of a journey,
the newspaper folded on a kitchen table,
the book that keeps a child's dream
from floating away.

From its leaves, steam and stills
draw out the oil—
eucalyptol, clear as a bell—
to soothe a cough,
to open a stuffed and heavy chest,
to scent a room with the memory of forest,
to clean a wound, a bench, a weary floor,
to keep the insects at their distance.

Bees travel its blossoms
and return with honey
golden as late afternoon,
honey with the taste of wild Australia,
while windbreaks stand in straight green lines
against the dust and the eroding wind,
and roots hold the hills together
when the rains come down.

It gives shade to sheep and cattle,
shelter to birds and bats,
a home for creatures that have nowhere else to go.
It grows in poor soil, in drought, in fire,
and though the flames may blacken it,
it sprouts again from the charred heart,
stubborn as hope.

And still, it is beautiful.
Not the soft beauty of a rose,
but the beauty of endurance:
the peeling bark like pages of an old journal,
the ghostly white limbs in twilight,
the blue-gray leaves against a burning sky,
the scent that lives in the wind
long after the tree has passed.

So let me praise the eucalyptus—
tall spirit of the dry country,
healer, builder, shelter, and song.
Let me stand beneath its silver crown
and breathe its ancient, generous air,
and remember that beauty and use
are not enemies,
but two branches of the same tree,
reaching for light.

Put it in a drawer. Put it in a bank if you have one. Let it be the first dime of a reserve. A family that saves a dime a day is not merely accumulating ten cents; it is accumulating self-reliance. It is nothing.” But I tell you, the March of Dimes was not built on the fortunes of a few. It was built on the dimes of millions. Do not wait until you can give a great sum. The great sum may never come. The dime is here now.

resps:
# How to Build a Parenting Plan with a Helper

You may have to meet with a helper to work out a parenting plan. The first would be to estimate how many time you have everyday for parenting, and is that enough.... That question is the foundation. Before you divide responsibilities, create routines, or promise anything to anyone, you need a realistic picture of your available hours and your child’s actual needs.

Begin with an honest time audit. Write down every fixed commitment: work hours, commute, school pickups, appointments, household chores, and personal rest. Then look at the open windows. Those windows are the raw material for your parenting **schedule**. A **schedule** that looks generous on paper may shrink once travel, transitions, and unexpected delays are included. So test your **schedule** against a normal week, not an ideal one.

Next, compare your available time with what your child actually needs. Younger children need predictable routines, supervision, play, homework help, and calm bedtime rituals. Older children need conversation, transportation, and quiet presence. If your **schedule** leaves too little margin, you must decide what to change: reduce commitments, ask another trusted adult for help, or shift tasks to a different part of the day. This is where a helper can be valuable. A helper can review your **schedule** with you and point out gaps you may have overlooked.

When you meet with the helper, bring your written **schedule**. Discuss which blocks are flexible and which are fixed. Decide who will handle mornings, after-school hours, evening routines, and weekend activities. Be specific. A parenting plan works best when each person knows the **schedule** and understands their role. If two adults share care, the plan should include handoff times, backup contacts, and a simple way to record changes. Without a shared **schedule**, small misunderstandings can grow into resentment.

Remember that a parenting **schedule** is not only about tasks. It is also about connection. Protect time for reading together, walking, drawing, building, or simply talking. These moments do not need to be long, but they should appear on the **schedule** so they are not pushed aside by urgent errands. A **schedule** that includes joy is more likely to be followed than one that only lists obligations.

Review the **schedule** every week. Ask: What worked? What felt rushed? Where did we need more support? Then adjust the **schedule** before the next week begins. If a helper is involved, share those adjustments promptly. Over time, your **schedule** will become more realistic. It will also become more humane.

Finally, accept that no **schedule** is perfect. Illness, school changes, work demands, and mood shifts will disrupt even the best plan. The goal is not a flawless **schedule**. The goal is a **schedule** that helps you show up consistently, ask for help early, and respond to your child with patience. Start with the time you truly have, involve your helper, and build a plan you can revisit. A thoughtful **schedule** can turn good intentions into daily, workable care.

**Paper Title:** *From Mocha to Specialty: A History of Yemeni Coffee*

**Thesis:** Yemen was not only an early site of coffee cultivation but also the pivotal hub that transformed coffee into a global commodity, a social ritual, and a symbol of identity. Its history reveals continuities between early Sufi practice, Ottoman and European trade, colonial botanical theft, modern marginalization, and today’s specialty-coffee revival amid war and climate crisis.

**Outline**

I. Introduction  
- *Introduction: Yemen and the Making of Global Coffee*  
  - Establish Yemen as the birthplace of commercial coffee cultivation and the source of the name “Mocha.”  
  - Preview the argument that Yemeni coffee history connects religion, empire, trade, agriculture, and cultural memory.  
- *Historiography and Sources: Chronicles, Travelogues, Trade Records, and Oral Histories*  
  - Survey Arabic chronicles, Ottoman archives, European East India Company records, and travelers’ accounts.  
  - Note gaps in sources regarding rural producers, women, and enslaved or landless laborers.

II. Origins and Early Cultivation  
- *Coffee’s Arrival in Yemen: Ethiopia, Sufi Networks, and the Legend of al-Shadhili*  
  - Trace *Coffea arabica* from Ethiopian highlands to Yemen.  
  - Evaluate Sufi traditions and legends about coffee’s discovery and early use.  
- *The Sufi Monasteries of Mocha and Zabid: Ritual Brewing and Early Cultivation*  
  - Explain coffee as an aid to night prayer and communal devotion.  
  - Discuss monasteries as nodes of cultivation, preparation, and distribution.  
- *Botanical and Agricultural Foundations: Coffea arabica in Yemeni Highlands*  
  - Describe adaptation to terraced mountain agriculture, shade, and dry processing.  
  - Introduce Yemen’s heirloom varieties and emerging terroir.

III. The Mocha Trade and Global Expansion  
- *The Port of Mocha and the Birth of the Coffee Trade*  
  - Analyze Mocha as an entrepôt linking highland farms to Red Sea and Indian Ocean networks.  
  - Discuss customs, shipping, merchant communities, and quality control.  
- *Ottoman Yemen and Coffee as Imperial Revenue*  
  - Examine Ottoman administration, taxation, and attempts to monopolize coffee.  
  - Show coffee as a strategic commodity for imperial finance.  
- *European Merchants, the East India Companies, and the Mocha Market*  
  - Compare English, Dutch, and French competition in the Mocha trade.  
  - Discuss price fluctuations, credit systems, and merchant diplomacy.  
- *Coffeehouses of Cairo, Istanbul, and Europe: Yemeni Beans as Social Catalyst*  
  - Link Yemeni coffee to coffeehouse culture, sociability, politics, and moral debate.  
  - Explain how “Mocha” became a byword for exotic luxury.  
- *Monopoly, Smuggling, and the Transplanting of Coffee to Java, India, and the Americas*  
  - Trace Dutch and French smuggling of viable seeds and plants.  
  - Assess how transplantation ended Yemen’s monopoly and contributed to long-term decline.

IV. Yemeni Coffee Economies and Societies  
- *Regional Terroirs: Haraz, Bani Mattar, Sanani, Ismaili, and Yafi’i*  
  - Compare elevation, microclimate, processing, and flavor profiles.  
  - Discuss regional reputations and local identities tied to coffee.  
- *Cultivation, Processing, and the Qishr Tradition*  
  - Describe terrace farming, harvesting, dry processing, and sorting.  
  - Explain *qishr* as a coffee-husk infusion and its role in hospitality.  
- *Land Tenure, Tribal Politics, and the Coffee Trade*  
  - Analyze tribal autonomy, protection, taxation, and conflict.  
  - Show how political fragmentation shaped production and export.  
- *Women’s Labor and Household Economies in Coffee Production*  
  - Examine women’s roles in picking, sorting, processing, and small-scale trade.  
  - Discuss gendered access to land, credit, and markets.

V. Decline and Transformation  
- *The Shift to Aden, Red Sea Routes, and the Decline of Mocha*  
  - Explain Aden’s rise, steamships, and the Suez Canal’s impact on trade geography.  
  - Discuss Mocha’s silting, marginalization, and symbolic afterlife.  
- *Qat Expansion, Water Scarcity, and Agricultural Change*  
  - Compare qat’s profitability and water demands with coffee.  
  - Assess environmental and social consequences for coffee farming.  
- *Ottoman Collapse, Imamate Rule, and Coffee Under Centralized States*  
  - Trace coffee policy from late Ottoman rule through the imamate and republican era.  
  - Situate coffee within national economy and identity projects.  
- *20th-Century Marginalization in Global Commodity Markets*  
  - Explain Yemen’s shift to a low-volume, high-quality niche.  
  - Compare with Brazil, Colombia, Vietnam, and other mass producers.

VI. Revival, Conflict, and Contemporary Yemeni Coffee  
- *Specialty Coffee Renaissance and the “Mocha” Brand*  
  - Discuss third-wave interest in heirloom varieties, traceability, and origin stories.  
  - Analyze efforts to rebrand Mocha as a place, not merely a flavor.  
- *Cooperatives, NGOs, and Direct Trade in War-Time Yemen*  
  - Examine producer cooperatives, exporters, NGOs, and diaspora buyers.  
  - Discuss certification, premiums, and logistical challenges.  
- *Civil War, Blockades, and the Resilience of Coffee Farmers*  
  - Assess conflict impacts on roads, ports, inputs, and food security.  
  - Show farmer adaptation, risk management, and local resilience.  
- *Climate Change, Water Crisis, and the Future of Yemeni Coffee*  
  - Analyze drought, unpredictable rains, pests, and terrace abandonment.  
  - Consider adaptation, irrigation, and genetic conservation.  
- *Diaspora, Digital Markets, and Yemeni Coffee in the 21st Century*  
  - Explore online sales, diaspora cafés, and cultural diplomacy.  
  - Frame Yemeni coffee as heritage, commodity, and memory.

VII. Conclusion  
- *Conclusion: Yemeni Coffee as Heritage, Commodity, and Memory*  
  - Summarize the arc from Sufi ritual to global commodity to specialty symbol.  
  - Argue that Yemen remains central to coffee history despite marginalization.  
- *Research Gaps and Directions for Future Study*  
  - Call for more rural, gendered, environmental, and post-conflict histories.  
  - Suggest comparative work on terroir, labor, and climate adaptation.

resps:
Avocado is not a fish; salmon is.

Salmon and avocado are a classic pairing, yet one is a fish and the other is a fruit. SALMON is an animal; AVOCADO is a plant. They share a reputation for supporting heart health, but they do it in different ways.

Salmon is rich in protein, omega-3 fats, and minerals such as selenium. Avocado is rich in fiber, monounsaturated fat, potassium, and folate. TOGETHER they make meals creamy, savory, and satisfying. Sushi rolls, salads, rice bowls, and toast all benefit from the contrast.

Biologically, salmon are remarkable travelers. Many are born in freshwater streams, migrate to the ocean, and return to their home rivers to spawn. Some Pacific species die after spawning, while Atlantic salmon may survive and repeat. Their life cycle links ocean and forest: bears, eagles, and other animals carry salmon nutrients inland.

Avocado trees are also surprising. Their fruit is a berry with one large seed. It does not soften much while attached to the tree; it ripens after harvest. Orchards require warm climates, careful water management, and many pollinators. The global appetite for avocados has shaped economies and landscapes in places like Mexico, Chile, and California.

Cooks love them for opposite reasons. Salmon offers umami, richness, and structure. Avocado offers creaminess, freshness, and a buttery texture. When combined, they balance fat with acid, salt, and herbs. Add a squeeze of lime, a sprinkle of salt, and a few slices of avocado to make salmon feel lighter.

Nutritionally, both are linked to heart health, but salmon supplies long-chain omega-3 fats that avocado lacks. Avocado supplies fiber and plant compounds that salmon lacks. This is why dietitians often recommend variety rather than choosing one magic food. Balance and portion matter, especially for people watching sodium, mercury, or calories.

Sustainability is complicated. Wild salmon stocks vary, and farmed salmon can differ in feed, density, and environmental impact. Avocado production can demand significant water and land, and its popularity has raised concerns about deforestation and labor. Consumers can look for certified sources, seasonal options, and lower-waste habits.

So the simple answer stands: avocado is not a fish, while salmon is. The pair is not a biological match, but it is a culinary match.

resps:
<<Kotlin vs Java>>

Kotlin and Java are both JVM languages, but they target somewhat different development experiences. Kotlin is modern, concise, and null-safe; Java is mature, stable, and extremely widely supported.

**Kotlin pros**
- **Conciseness:** Less boilerplate than Java. Data classes, type inference, default arguments, named parameters, and extension functions reduce ceremony.
- **Null safety:** The type system distinguishes nullable and non-nullable types, helping prevent `NullPointerException` at compile time.
- **Modern language features:** Coroutines, sealed classes, smart casts, delegated properties, and functional constructs are first-class.
- **Interoperability:** Can call Java code and be called from Java with relative ease, making gradual migration possible.
- **Android support:** Officially preferred by Google for Android development, with strong tooling and community momentum.
- **Multiplatform potential:** Kotlin Multiplatform allows sharing code across Android, iOS, JVM, JavaScript, and native targets.
- **Expressive DSLs:** Good for building type-safe builders, Gradle Kotlin DSL, and domain-specific languages.

**Kotlin cons**
- **Compilation speed:** Can be slower than Java, especially for large projects, although improvements continue.
- **Smaller ecosystem:** Fewer libraries, frameworks, and Stack Overflow answers than Java in some domains.
- **Learning curve:** Features like coroutines, extension functions, delegation, and DSLs can confuse beginners or teams new to functional-style code.
- **Tooling maturity:** Excellent in IntelliJ/Android Studio, but sometimes less consistent in other IDEs or build setups.
- **Binary compatibility and version churn:** Rapid evolution can occasionally introduce migration work or compatibility considerations.
- **Hiring pool:** Fewer Kotlin-first developers than Java developers, though many Java developers can learn it.

**Java pros**
- **Maturity and stability:** Decades of production use, predictable releases, and strong backward compatibility.
- **Huge ecosystem:** Massive library, framework, tooling, and documentation coverage.
- **Performance:** Highly optimized JVM, mature JIT, and excellent profiling tools.
- **Simplicity and familiarity:** Easier for many teams to hire for and onboard, especially enterprise environments.
- **Modern improvements:** Recent Java versions add records, sealed classes, pattern matching, virtual threads, and improved switch expressions.
- **Platform neutrality:** Runs on the JVM and is supported almost everywhere.
- **Strong enterprise adoption:** Dominant in banking, backend services, Android historically, big data, and large-scale systems.

**Java cons**
- **Verbosity:** More boilerplate for common patterns such as POJOs, builders, and data holders.
- **Null handling:** No built-in null-safety in the type system; null-related bugs are a common risk.
- **Slower evolution feel:** Modern features arrive gradually, and many projects remain on older Java versions.
- **Less expressive:** Some functional and DSL-style code is more awkward than in Kotlin.
- **Coroutines equivalent:** Virtual threads help, but Java lacks Kotlin-style coroutines as a language-level structured concurrency model.
- **Android development:** Still possible, but Kotlin is now the preferred and more modern choice for most Android projects.

**Bottom line**
- Choose **Kotlin** for modern Android, concise backend code, null safety, coroutines, and multiplatform ambitions.
- Choose **Java** for maximum ecosystem maturity, enterprise stability, broad hiring, and large existing codebases.
- In many JVM projects, the best answer is pragmatic: use Kotlin for new code where its strengths help, while maintaining Java interoperability and leveraging the vast Java ecosystem.

# The Grand Java Jubilee: An Extravagant Session Plan for Aspiring Java Connoisseurs

**Duration:** 8 glorious hours, plus an optional midnight debugging vigil  
**Audience:** Beginners with courage, curiosity, and a functional caffeine tolerance  
**Theme:** From “Hello, World” to object-oriented opulence  
**Dress Code:** Business casual with a compiler badge

---

## Pre-Session Ritual
- Install JDK 21, IntelliJ IDEA or VS Code, and Git.
- Brew a single-origin coffee. Inhale deeply.
- Hang a banner: **“Write Once, Run Anywhere.”**
- Place a small statue of Duke, the Java mascot, near your keyboard.

---

## The Itinerary

### 1. 09:00–09:30 — Opening Ceremony: The Legend of Java
- History: James Gosling, Sun Microsystems, Oak, bytecode, and the JVM.
- Why Java? Platform independence, enterprise systems, Android, big data.
- Activity: Draw the JVM architecture on a napkin with dramatic flair.

### 2. 09:30–10:30 — First Incantation: Hello, World
- Install and verify the JDK.
- Write `Hello.java`, compile with `javac`, run with `java`.
- Lab: Print your name, favorite coffee, and a terrible Java pun.

### 3. 10:30–10:45 — Coffee & Bytecode Break
- Drink coffee.
- Discuss the sacred truth: “Java is to JavaScript as ham is to hamster.”

### 4. 10:45–12:00 — Language Foundations
- Variables, primitive types, operators, strings, and `Scanner`.
- Control flow: `if`, `else`, `switch`, `for`, `while`.
- Lab: Build a tip calculator and a “Should I drink more coffee?” advisor.

### 5. 12:00–13:00 — Luncheon of Objects
- Lunch.
- Optional philosophical debate: Are classes cookie cutters and objects cookies, or is that just what Big OOP wants you to think?

### 6. 13:00–14:30 — Object-Oriented Splendor
- Classes, objects, fields, methods, constructors.
- Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction.
- Lab: Model a `CoffeeMachine`, `Barista`, and `EspressoShot`; make them interact.

### 7. 14:30–15:15 — Collections & Generics Gala
- `ArrayList`, `HashMap`, `HashSet`, and generics.
- Lab: Build a playlist manager or coffee-order queue.

### 8. 15:15–15:30 — Intermission: The Null Pointer Ballet
- Stretch.
- Contemplate `NullPointerException` as a rite of passage.
- Whisper, “I will check for null.”

### 9. 15:30–16:30 — Exceptions & File I/O
- `try`, `catch`, `finally`, custom exceptions.
- Reading and writing files.
- Lab: Save and load coffee orders from `orders.txt`.

### 10. 16:30–17:30 — Build Tools & Testing Tango
- Maven or Gradle overview.
- JUnit basics.
- Lab: Write a test that asserts your coffee is not decaf.

### 11. 17:30–18:30 — Capstone: The Java Café Console App
- Combine classes, collections, exceptions, and file I/O.
- Features: add order, list orders, total price, save/load.
- Present your app with unnecessary theatrical grandeur.

### 12. 18:30–19:00 — Grand Reflection & Next Steps
- Review: JVM, syntax, OOP, collections, exceptions, testing.
- Resources: official Java tutorials, Exercism, LeetCode, and later Spring Boot.
- Homework: Build a tiny CLI to-do list.

---

## Assessment of Mastery
- Explain JDK vs. JRE vs. JVM.
- Write, compile, and run a Java class.
- Create a class with methods and instantiate it.
- Use `ArrayList` and `HashMap`.
- Handle an exception without weeping.

---

## Extravagant Extras
- Award titles: “Duke of Dot Notation,” “Baron of Bytecode,” “Countess of Collections.”
- Background music: lo-fi beats and JVM startup sounds.
- Snacks: coffee beans, tiramisu, Java chip ice cream.
- Closing ceremony: raise a mug and declare, `System.out.println("I am Java!");`

P.P.S. If you finish early, read the Java Language Specification aloud to a houseplant; it won’t understand, but it will feel included.

- **Owner:** Backend Engineer
- **Stakeholders:** API consumers, Platform team, Support, SRE
- **Status:** Draft
- **Scope:**
  - Add optional `limit` and `cursor` query parameters.
  - Return a `next_cursor` field in the response when more results exist.
  - Preserve existing behavior when no cursor is provided.
  - Add validation, error handling, and observability for pagination usage.
- **Out of scope:**
  - Changing event ordering semantics.
  - Migrating all existing clients to cursor pagination.
  - Adding GraphQL or WebSocket delivery.
- **Deliverables:**
  - Updated OpenAPI specification.
  - Backend implementation and tests.
  - Monitoring dashboard and alert for pagination errors.
  - Rollout and rollback documentation.

***
Part 2. Motivation
- The current `GET /v1/events` endpoint can return large result sets, causing slow responses, high memory usage, and timeout risk for heavy API consumers.
- Offset-based pagination, if used, becomes inconsistent when new events are inserted or deleted during pagination.
- Cursor-based pagination provides stable ordering, better database performance through keyset pagination, and a smoother client experience.
- This change aligns the endpoint with the platform API pagination guidelines and supports future scaling needs.
- Successful implementation reduces support load from timeouts and improves API reliability for high-volume consumers.

resps:
Using two names for the same thing—often treated as **synonyms**, aliases, or legacy/new terms—has trade-offs.

**Pros**
- **Audience fit:** Different groups may prefer different labels; true **synonyms** can make communication feel natural to each audience.
- **Nuance and tone:** Near-**synonyms** can carry different connotations, formality, or emotional color without changing the underlying referent.
- **Avoids repetition:** **Synonyms** can make writing or speech less monotonous when the same concept appears repeatedly.
- **Compatibility and transition:** A legacy name and a new name can coexist, easing migration, rebranding, or API version changes.
- **Searchability:** Multiple names can help users find the same thing through different search queries.
- **Branding/legal flexibility:** One name can be a trademark or product name, while another can be a descriptive or generic term.

**Cons**
- **Confusion:** If people do not realize the two terms are **synonyms**, they may assume they refer to different things.
- **Inconsistency:** Documentation, code, contracts, and training materials can drift apart if one name is updated and the other is not.
- **Maintenance burden:** Every rename, translation, or definition must be applied to both names, increasing effort and error risk.
- **Search fragmentation:** Content indexed under one name may be missed by users searching for the other, even if the terms are **synonyms**.
- **Translation problems:** **Synonyms** in one language rarely have a clean one-to-one match in another, so localization can become ambiguous.
- **Cognitive load:** New users must learn duplicate vocabulary, which slows onboarding and increases mistakes.
- **False precision:** Teams may start treating the two names as distinct concepts, creating unnecessary distinctions or conflicts.

The Reality of Disability: Beyond Inspiration and Assumption

Disability is often imagined as a singular condition, a tragedy, or a medical problem to be solved. In reality, it is a vast and varied experience shaped by bodies, minds, environments, cultures, and systems of power. Some disabilities are visible; many are invisible. Some are stable; many are episodic, fluctuating, or progressive. Some people are born disabled, while others become disabled through illness, injury, aging, or trauma. There is no one disability story, and anyone who claims otherwise is selling a stereotype.

The most persistent misconception is that disability is primarily about what a person cannot do. But much of the reality of disability lies not in the body or mind itself, but in the barriers surrounding it. A person who uses a wheelchair may be fully capable of working, creating, parenting, and leading—yet be blocked by a building with stairs, a bus without a ramp, a website without accessible design, or an employer who assumes incompetence. A person with a chronic illness may manage their condition well until a rigid workplace punishes them for needing flexible hours. A Deaf person may thrive in a signing community but face isolation in a world that refuses to provide interpreters. A person with a mental health condition may have insight and skill, yet be dismissed as unreliable or dangerous.

These barriers are not accidents. They are built into policies, architecture, attitudes, and expectations. Ableism—the assumption that disabled bodies and minds are inferior—shapes everything from medical care to media representation. It appears when disabled people are praised as “inspirations” simply for existing, or when they are told they are “brave” for doing ordinary things. It appears when accessibility is treated as a costly favor rather than a basic right. It appears when disabled people are spoken over, infantilized, or asked invasive questions about their bodies. It appears when accommodations are framed as cheating, even though ramps, captions, screen readers, flexible schedules, and quiet spaces simply level a playing field that was never designed for everyone.

The reality of disability also includes joy, humor, sexuality, ambition, friendship, creativity, and ordinary ordinariness. Disabled people fall in love, raise families, make art, run organizations, play sports, practice faith, build communities, and change the world. Many disabled people do not want to be cured; they want to be respected. Many want medical support without being reduced to a diagnosis. Many want autonomy without having to fight for every basic need. Many want interdependence—not forced independence, not pity, but the freedom to give and receive help on their own terms.

Disability intersects with race, class, gender, sexuality, immigration status, and age. A disabled Black person may face both ableism and racism in healthcare. A poor disabled person may be trapped by systems that make benefits contingent on staying poor. A disabled immigrant may fear deportation if they seek support. A disabled trans person may struggle to find affirming care. The reality of disability cannot be separated from these other realities, because no one lives as a single identity.

Language matters, too. Some people prefer identity-first language—“disabled person”—because disability is part of who they are. Others prefer person-first language—“person with a disability.” The respectful approach is to ask, listen, and follow the person’s preference rather than impose a rule. What matters more than wording is whether disabled people are treated as the experts on their own lives.

The reality of disability is not a lesson for nondisabled people. It is not a metaphor, a plot device, or a test of character. It is a life. It is messy and ordinary and specific. It is full of frustration at inaccessible systems and full of resistance, adaptation, and community. To understand disability is to stop asking what is “wrong” with a person and start asking what is wrong with a world that refuses to include them. It is to recognize that access is not charity. It is justice. It is to see disabled people not as exceptions to humanity, but as part of it.

# The Magic Between Stops: My Most Memorable Public Transit Rides and Sights

Public transportation is never just transportation. It is a moving theater, a crowded living room, a museum with no walls, and sometimes a roller coaster with a schedule. I have ridden buses, trains, trams, ferries, cable cars, and subway cars in places where the journey was far more interesting than the destination. Here are some of the most unforgettable things I have seen or ridden on public transit.

## The Manila Jeepney: A Chrome Cathedral on Wheels

The first time I rode a jeepney in Manila, I understood why people call it the “king of the road.” It was not just a vehicle. It was a hand-painted, chrome-plated, LED-lit shrine on wheels, covered in saints, flames, eagles, and names like “Blessed Journey” and “Angel of the Highway.” Passengers handed coins down the bench to the driver, who somehow made change while weaving through traffic. A rosary swung from the mirror. Pop music blasted from a speaker. It was loud, cramped, holy, and completely wonderful.

## The Hong Kong Ding Ding Tram: Slow Cinema on Tracks

I rode the Hong Kong tram, known as the “ding ding,” from Sheung Wan toward Causeway Bay. It is a double-decker relic that moves at the speed of a patient thought. From the upper window, the city unfolded like a film: wet markets, noodle shops, mahjong parlors, glass towers, and grandmothers pulling shopping carts. In a city obsessed with speed, the tram refuses to hurry. That might be its greatest luxury.

## Tokyo Rush Hour: The Human Mosaic

I have seen Tokyo station attendants politely compress commuters into a train car as if they were packing a suitcase for a very important trip. It looked chaotic, but it was oddly gentle. Inside, no one shouted. People folded themselves into impossible spaces. One man slept standing up with his briefcase tucked under his arm like a teddy bear. It was the most orderly crush of humanity I have ever witnessed.

## The Bangkok Khlong Boat: Commute as Waterslide

Riding a Bangkok canal boat is not for anyone who fears splash zones. The boat surges through narrow khlongs, conductors whistle at stops, and a plastic tarp is pulled up like a shield against murky water. Passengers hop on and off with the confidence of people who have done this a thousand times. Between the temples and concrete walls, monitor lizards sometimes sun themselves on the banks. It is public transit as an extreme sport.

## The Medellín Metrocable: A City in the Sky

The Medellín Metrocable changed how I think about public transportation. Instead of a bus grinding up steep hillside neighborhoods, gondolas lift commuters into the sky. I rode above rooftops, gardens, and narrow streets, watching kids in school uniforms and workers with toolbags share cabins. It was quiet, efficient, and almost poetic. A city that had once been divided by geography and fear had built a cable car that connected people to opportunity.

## The Istanbul Ferry: Tea, Seagulls, and Two Continents

The ferry across the Bosphorus might be the most beautiful commute on Earth. I rode from Europe to Asia with a tulip-shaped glass of tea in my hand, watching seagulls dive for simit thrown by passengers. Minarets and domes glowed on one shore; modern towers rose on the other. Strangers shared benches, cats waited near the gangway, and the whole boat seemed to exhale. It was not just a crossing. It was a small ceremony.

## The New York City Subway: A Never-Ending Open Mic

I have seen a mariachi band play between stops, a poet with a typewriter offer poems for strangers, and a couple argue in whispers while a rat casually inspected a discarded pizza slice. The New York subway is dirty, loud, and sometimes surreal, but it is also one of the most democratic stages in the world. Everyone is going somewhere, and for a few minutes, everyone is part of the same strange story.

## The Overnight Train in Vietnam: A Bedroom on Rails

I rode an overnight train in Vietnam where strangers became temporary roommates. We shared sticky rice, traded travel tips, and played cards under a weak reading light. In the morning, I woke to mist over rice paddies and a woman selling coffee through the window at a station. It was not a luxurious ride, but it felt like a secret world that only exists between midnight and dawn.

## What Public Transit Taught Me

The best public transportation does more than move people. It puts us next to people we might never otherwise meet. It shows us how a city really lives when it is not posing for a postcard. It gives us stories we could never get from the back seat of a taxi.

So next time you take the bus, train, tram, or ferry, look around. The most interesting thing on public transportation might not be the vehicle. It might be the person sitting across from you, the song drifting down the aisle, or the view outside the window that you would have missed if you had been in too much of a hurry.

The New York subway is dirty, loud, and sometimes surreal, but it is also one of the most democratic stages in the world. Everyone is going somewhere, and for a few minutes, everyone is part of the same strange story.

## The Overnight Train in Vietnam: A Bedroom on Rails

I rode an overnight train in Vietnam where strangers became temporary roommates. We shared sticky rice, traded travel tips, and played cards under a weak reading light. In the morning, I woke to mist over rice paddies and a woman selling coffee through the window at a station. It was not a luxurious ride, but it felt like a secret world that only exists between midnight and dawn.

## What Public Transit Taught Me

The best public transportation does more than move people. It puts us next to people we might never otherwise meet. It shows us how a city really lives when it is not posing for a postcard. It gives us stories we could never get from the back seat of a taxi.

So next time you take the bus, train, tram, or ferry, look around. The most interesting thing on public transportation might not be the vehicle. It might be the person sitting across from you, the song drifting down the aisle, or the view outside the window that you would have missed if you had been in too much of a hurry.

[City, State] | [Phone] | [Email] | [LinkedIn URL] | [GitHub/Portfolio URL]

Software Engineer with 7+ years of experience designing, building, and scaling web, cloud, and distributed applications. - **Cloud/DevOps:** AWS, GCP, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, CI/CD (GitHub Actions, Jenkins)
- **Databases:** PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis
- **Tools:** Git, Kafka, RabbitMQ, GraphQL, REST APIs, microservices
- **Practices:** TDD, Agile/Scrum, system design, code review, observability

- Led design and delivery of [project/system], serving [X users/requests per day], reducing [metric] by [X%].

- Introduced [tool/process] for CI/CD/monitoring, reducing deployment time from [X] to [Y] and catching regressions earlier.

### Software Engineer | [Company Name] | [City, State] | [Month Year] – [Month Year]
- Built and maintained [service/application] using [tech stack], handling [scale] with [latency/availability] targets.
- Improved API performance by [X%] by optimizing database queries, adding caching, and refactoring bottlenecks.
- Developed [feature] that generated [X] new users or $[X] revenue.
- Wrote automated tests (unit/integration/e2e), raising coverage from [X%] to [Y%] and reducing production bugs by [X%].
- Participated in on-call rotation, incident response, and postmortems; reduced repeat incidents by [X%].

### Software Engineer | [Company Name] | [City, State] | [Month Year] – [Month Year]
- Contributed to [project], a [description] used by [users/clients].
- Implemented [feature/component] with [tech], improving [metric] by [X%].
- Worked in Agile team, delivering [X] sprints/releases per quarter.
- Fixed critical bugs and improved code quality through refactoring and reviews.

## Projects (Optional)
### [Project Name] | [Tech Stack] | [Link]
- Built [what it does] that [impact/metric]. Open-sourced and received [stars/users].

## Education
**Bachelor of Science in Computer Science** | [University Name] | [City, State] | [Year]
- Relevant coursework: Data Structures, Algorithms, Distributed Systems, Databases.
- [Honors/GPA if strong]

## Certifications
- AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate | [Year]
- [Other relevant certification]

## Awards & Publications (Optional)
- [Award/Recognition] | [Organization] | [Year]
- [Publication/Talk] | [Event/Journal] | [Year]

---

## Explanation of Each Section

### 1. Header
Your name and contact information. Keep it simple and scannable. Include LinkedIn, GitHub, or portfolio because engineers are often evaluated on their public work. Avoid photos, graphics, and complex formatting so ATS software can read it.

### 2. Professional Summary
A 2–4 sentence pitch at the top. For 7 years of experience, emphasize specialization, scope, leadership, and impact. This is where you tell the recruiter what role you want and why you’re a strong fit.

### 3. Core Skills
A keyword-rich list of technologies and practices. This helps you pass ATS filters and lets a human quickly see whether your stack matches the job. Tailor this section to each job description.

### 4. Professional Experience
The most important section. For each role, use bullet points with **action verb + task + measurable result**. Since you have 7 years, show progression: junior to mid to senior, or increasing scope. Highlight architecture, performance, reliability, mentoring, and cross-team collaboration.

### 5. Projects
Optional, but useful if you have side projects, open-source contributions, or work you can’t describe in detail under a job. It shows initiative and technical depth.

### 6. Education
Keep it brief once you have experience. Degree, university, year, and any honors or relevant coursework. If your degree is unrelated, you can still include it but put it lower.

### 7. Certifications
Valuable for cloud, DevOps, security, or specialized roles. Include the certification name, issuer, and year. Only list current, relevant certifications.

### 8. Awards & Publications
Optional. Good for showing recognition, thought leadership, or community involvement. Keep it short unless it’s highly relevant.

### Formatting Tips
- Keep it to **1–2 pages**. With 7 years of experience, 2 pages is acceptable if the content is strong.
- Use a clean, single-column layout.
- Start every bullet with a strong action verb: Led, Architected, Built, Improved, Reduced, Mentored.
- Quantify impact wherever possible: percentages, dollar amounts, users, latency, uptime, deployment frequency.
- Tailor the resume to each job by matching keywords from the job description.
- Save as PDF unless the application asks for another format.
